vignette:
Aroha is sixty-five years old. She wears her silver hair pulled back in a neat ponytail, and her hands, though stiff with arthritis, move across the laptop keyboard in session with a deliberate precision that suggests she is still searching for a keystroke that might undo the past eighteen months.

Before the accident, she was a long-distance cyclist. She used to say it was the only time her mind went quiet. The rhythm of her breath, the burn in her thighs, the coastal road unfurling beneath her—it was a meditation her husband, Tama, had encouraged her to take up during his illness. After he passed from cancer five years ago, the bicycle became more than a hobby. It was a ritual. A discipline. She woke at five in the morning, rode the Kāpiti Coast route for forty kilometers, showered, and drove to work. Order. Control. These were the bedrock of her life.

The accident happened on a clear morning. A logging truck. The driver fell asleep at the wheel. When Aroha tells this story, she does not focus on the pain of the broken pelvis or the shattered wrist. She describes the geometry of the failure. “I was in the correct position. I had the high-vis vest. The sun was at my back. The variables were optimal. And still, a thirty-ton truck took my handlebars off.”

She remembers the sound. Carbon fiber splintering against the asphalt. The smell of hot tar and diesel. She remembers lying in the ditch, her body ringing like a struck bell, her mind performing a rapid diagnostic. Am I paralyzed? Can I breathe? Where is the blood coming from? She focused on a single leaf of a ponga fern, using it as an anchor to keep from slipping into shock. She remembers the silence after the truck finally stopped a hundred meters down the road. That silence was identical to the silence in the hospital room when the doctor had told her Tama was gone.

Now, she does not cycle. The bike is in the garage, covered in a dusty tarp. She does not drive the coastal road. She takes an inland route that adds forty minutes to her commute, winding through the suburbs. She tells her mokopuna that Nanny’s bones are too old for the road now. But the real reason is that the sound of any engine braking at speed causes her throat to close.

At work, she is a senior cybersecurity analyst. Before the accident, she was known for her unshakable calm. She could sit in the middle of a live ransomware attack and dismantle the threat piece by piece. She specialized in pattern recognition. “The bad guys always leave a signature,” she used to say. But the accident broke her pattern language. The signature of the trauma is everywhere. She cannot sit with her back to the door in the office cafeteria. She startles when her phone pings in a rhythm that reminds her of a reversing beeper. Her sleep is a battlefield; she works late into the night because the quiet hum of the server room is the only place she feels a semblance of safety.

Her mood is a wall. She watches her grandchildren play, but the joy feels like a photograph of a feeling rather than the feeling itself. She has stopped going to the marae. The karanga, the spiritual welcome which once felt like a net catching her soul, now feels like a demand she cannot meet. She carries a persistent sense of doom, as if a flaw has been introduced into the code of the universe, and she is the only one who can see it. She is irritable with her junior team. “You missed that vulnerability in the firewall. Do you want someone to die?” She knows the words are too big for the context, but she cannot hold them back.

She describes her symptoms to me like a system report. “Intrusive memories: daily. Hypervigilance: constant. Avoidance: severe. Negative beliefs about the world: total.”

But the tears come when she talks about the silence. “I built a world around order. I grieved Tama with order. I worked with order. I filled every moment of the day. That truck proved it was all a fragile lie. The road was never safe. The air was never safe. I have always been one small piece of bad luck away from that ditch. And now I cannot unsee it.”

She sits across from me, a brilliant woman who analyzed threats for a living, now held hostage by the memory of a single, unmanageable second. She is not looking for me to name the wound. She already knows its name. She is sitting in the wreckage of the world she built, trying to understand how a world built on logic could be erased by pure, dumb chance.
